title: Shared Involvement

outline.heading: Macro Phase: Socializing in Game Worlds
outline.summary: Calleja opens by historicizing multiplayer gaming from pre-digital public-space play through two-player home consoles, LAN parties, and console-integrated multiplayer (PlayStation Home). MMOGs anchor the macro phase: persistent globally-distributed populations create full-fledged online societies (friendships, marriages, betrayals — EVE Online Guiding Hand Social Club heist exemplifies the latter). Citing Steinkuehler & Williams (2006), Taylor (2006), Castronova (2005), and Klastrup (2004), Calleja argues that MMOGs differ from chat rooms by furnishing goal-directed activity that contextualizes communication; end-game content makes guilds prerequisite, and geographically-organized guilds (Austin Texas WoW example) bleed into out-of-game sociality.

outline.heading: Governance in Massively Multiplayer On-line Games
outline.summary: Sustained case-study (pp.97-99): the Sara Andrews / Blizzard Entertainment incident (January 2006) — a player forming a WoW guild welcoming gay men, lesbians, and transsexuals is warned by Blizzard for violating Terms of Use 'Harassment — Sexual Orientation.' Calleja reads this as exposing the magic-circle concept as dangerous when applied to MMOG governance: corporations like Blizzard adopt the magic-circle posture to cordon off virtual worlds from real-world social concerns, but server-consensus self-policing means practical enforcement is dictated by majority chat behavior, not corporate intent. He then turns (pp.99-100) to Oldenburg's (1999) 'third places' and Steinkuehler & Williams's (2006) ethnographic test (Lineage / Lineage 2 / Asheron's Call / Asheron's Call 2) finding MMOGs fit most third-place criteria — better at bridging than bonding social capital.

outline.heading: Micro Phase: Collaboration, Competition, and Cohabitation during Gameplay
outline.summary: Bridge passage analogizing game agents to literary/film characters but noting agents in games carry coded behavioral, psychological, and physical properties (Spore one-eyed rhinos example). Human-controlled agents shift this further — avatars in WoW's Ironforge are improv-theater actors in a larger environment. Player disposition reorients once human/AI distinction is recognized. Authorial enumeration slip at p.101: 'there are four dimensions of shared involvement: cohabitation, competition, and cooperation' — list contains three, three subsections follow.

outline.heading: Cohabitation
outline.summary: Cohabitation anchors the player spatially and socially in a living environment. Even rudimentary AI suffices to evoke cohabitation (Gerhard, Moore & Hobbs 2004), per Reeves & Nass's (1996) media-equation thesis that media interfaces are treated as social actors automatically and unconsciously, plus Calo (2010) on sociality of computer-controlled agents. GTA IV's Dimitri Rascalov betrayal of Nico Bellic is processed as betrayal-by-mobster, not interaction-with-program. MMOG persistence layers reputation onto cohabitation (kill-on-sight lists; ninja-looting; ganking). Cohabitation includes spectatorship: clan trials via spectator-mode screening; co-located console FIFA 2009 living-room scenarios where actions become performance-for-audience, prompting visually-pleasing rather than goal-directed play.

outline.heading: Cooperation
outline.summary: Cooperation (Manninen & Kujanpaa 2005; Heide-Smith 2007) emerges in co-op (Halo 3 split-screen), LAN gaming, designed-interdependence games (Left 4 Dead AI director, Hunter/Smoker mechanics requiring teammate rescue; visible-through-walls cohesion device; shared single-use medical pack), and MMOG group/guild structures (5–6 person groups scaling to 15/20/40-person raid groups using TeamSpeak or Ventrilo). Planetside participants emphasized mass-collaboration memorable sessions; WoW PvE participants foregrounded collaboration over PvP. All but two participants cited interaction with others as primary MMOG motivation.

outline.heading: Competition and Conflict
outline.summary: Caillois (1962) 'agon' frames competition; digital games scale agon to globally-distributed real-time contests (paradigm shift). Range: Pong/Combat synchronous 2-player → split-screen Gran Turismo → same-screen FIFA 2009 → simultaneous cooperate-while-competing Rock Band. Conflict can occur between parties with differing goals (LOTRO Bree–Rivendell journey; Angmar quest collisions). AI conflict in Half-Life 2 / S.T.A.L.K.E.R. — adaptive yet predictable relative to Space Invaders baseline. Malaby's (2007) social contingency (codependent on performative contingency) explains preference for human opponents (BunkerBoy86 Planetside quote). AI limitations: Empire: Total War units act on local triggers without holistic battlefield awareness; FPS bots show pinpoint accuracy yet fail traps. Lim & Reeves (2006) document heightened arousal/engagement vs AI. Competitive FPS (Counter-Strike, Call of Duty IV, Red Orchestra) sustains the casual→clan→semipro arc (Rambusch, Pargman & Jakobsson 2007: shift from individual to team play). Shared involvement, like other dimensions, can be conscious or internalized — and cooperation/competition demand semi-conscious learning before mastery.

dimension_operational_definition: Shared involvement is the engagement derived from awareness of and interaction with other agents in a game environment, whether human- or computer-controlled, encompassing cohabitation, cooperation, and competition; it spans macro-phase persistent online sociality (guild and community life across sessions) and micro-phase moment-to-moment co-presence, collaboration, and contest during gameplay.
boundary_criteria: Agent-other-than-self condition: the dimension is engaged only where the player perceives another agent (human or sufficiently coded AI) inhabiting the same environment — distinguishing it from purely spatial habitation (IG-05) where the environment may be empty.

Awareness-and-interaction condition (not pure co-presence): the engagement requires perceived interaction-potential or actual interaction, not merely background avatar density — though Calleja allows ambient cohabitation as a minimal-threshold case.

Social-versus-functional valence: the dimension foregrounds social bond, reputation, performance-for-audience, or contest-with-another, distinguishing it from the kinesthetic (IG-04) procedural-motor axis and ludic (IG-09) rule-goal axis even when sociality is the operational vehicle for those axes.

Persistence-sensitive: macro-phase shared involvement requires environment persistence such that reputation, friendship, betrayal accumulate across sessions — distinguishing MMOG cases from one-off LAN matches even where both involve human others.

Indifferent to medium of communication: chat, voice (Ventrilo/TeamSpeak), avatar gesture, and co-located vocal banter all count as shared-involvement channels — distinguishing it from narrative involvement (IG-07) where channel-of-delivery is constitutive.

concepts.label: macro-phase MMOG socializing
concepts.gloss: Persistent online sociality across sessions: friendships, marriages, betrayals, geographically-organized guilds, end-game prerequisites.

concepts.label: MMOGs as full-fledged on-line societies
concepts.gloss: Calleja's positional claim: MMOGs do not just host gameplay but constitute societies where social ties and tensions cross over into the everyday.

concepts.label: guilds and end-game content prerequisite
concepts.gloss: Calleja's structural observation: end-game content design forces guild formation, creating durable social bonds via repeated interdependent play.

concepts.label: out-of-game friendships / geographically-organized guilds
concepts.gloss: Real-world social spillover (Splate moved cross-country to live with MUD friends; Austin Texas WoW guild gatherings).

concepts.label: MMOG governance / Terms-of-Use enforcement
concepts.gloss: Corporate-platform exercise of behavioral policy on virtual-world populations — operationalized via the Sara Andrews / Blizzard case study.

concepts.label: magic-circle critique applied to MMOG governance
concepts.gloss: Calleja's argumentative target: the magic-circle posture becomes 'dangerous' when wielded by platform owners to cordon MMOGs off from real-world social concerns.

concepts.label: server-consensus enforcement / self-policing chat
concepts.gloss: Practical enforcement is dictated by majority chat behavior reporting one another — not by corporate policy alone.

concepts.label: MMOGs as third places (Oldenburg)
concepts.gloss: Steinkuehler & Williams's adaptation of Oldenburg's third-place criteria to virtual worlds: informal public gathering compensating for decline of off-line third spaces.

concepts.label: bridging vs bonding social capital
concepts.gloss: Steinkuehler & Williams conclusion: MMOGs better at broad cross-background bridging than deep emotional bonding — yet Oldenburg's complaint targets the bridging deficit, so MMOGs answer that need.

concepts.label: micro-phase cohabitation/cooperation/competition
concepts.gloss: Three subdimensions of moment-to-moment shared involvement during gameplay.

concepts.label: human-controlled vs computer-controlled agent distinction
concepts.gloss: Player disposition reorients once human/AI status of an agent is recognized; perception of co-presence-with-other-human alters experiential weight.

concepts.label: cohabitation as anchoring presence
concepts.gloss: Avatars walking and talking in a living city obfuscate the simulation-character of the environment, anchoring the player both spatially and socially.

concepts.label: media equation / computers as social actors
concepts.gloss: Reeves & Nass (1996): media interfaces treated as social actors automatically, unconsciously, at minimal cues.

concepts.label: persistent reputation in MMOGs
concepts.gloss: Kill-on-sight lists, ninja-looting flagging, ganking-reputation tracking — names persist; standing impacts gameplay decisions.

concepts.label: spectatorship and performance-for-audience
concepts.gloss: Spectator-mode in multiplayer transforms play into performance; co-located living-room FIFA 2009 audiences shift play from goal-directed to visually-pleasing action.

concepts.label: clans, trials, spectator-mode screening
concepts.gloss: Clan-entry trials use spectator-mode to assess applicant skill — institutionalized spectatorship feeding reputation economy.

concepts.label: co-op / LAN / split-screen cooperative play
concepts.gloss: Cooperative configurations from same-screen Halo 3 to LAN-hall tournaments — physical co-location enables verbal and gestural coordination.

concepts.label: designed interdependence (Left 4 Dead AI director)
concepts.gloss: Game-design choices (AI director tension management; Hunter/Smoker rescue-required attacks; see-through-walls visualization; single-use shared medical pack) engineer mandatory collaboration.

concepts.label: MMOG group and guild scaffolding
concepts.gloss: 5–6 person groups scaling to 15/20/40-person raid groups, sustained via guild chat plus TeamSpeak/Ventrilo voice infrastructure.

concepts.label: agon / competition typology (Caillois)
concepts.gloss: Caillois's (1962) agonistic-game category, scaled by digital games to globally-distributed real-time contests.

concepts.label: conflict-without-shared-goal
concepts.gloss: Calleja distinguishes direct-competition (shared goal, opposed factions) from conflict (differing objectives intersecting in environment — LOTRO Bree–Rivendell, Angmar).

concepts.label: social contingency (Malaby) codependent on performative contingency
concepts.gloss: Malaby's (2007) account of opponent-unpredictability as a key competition-contingency, requiring action on guesses (not just guessing).

concepts.label: AI agent limitations: pinpoint accuracy without holistic awareness
concepts.gloss: Empire: Total War units act on local triggers without battlefield-scale strategy; FPS bots show inhuman accuracy yet fall to player traps; Space Invaders is the predictable-AI baseline.

concepts.label: shift from individual to team play in competitive FPS clans
concepts.gloss: Rambusch, Pargman & Jakobsson (2007): casual→clan→semi-pro arc reshapes self-perception from individual to team-player; clan trials and team training; LAN tournaments.

concepts.label: internalization of shared involvement (conscious to mastery)
concepts.gloss: Like other PIM dimensions, shared involvement can be consciously attended or internalized; cooperation and competition both demand learning before mastery.

concepts.label: kinesthetic-prerequisite to social-contingency mapping
concepts.gloss: Attentional bridge to IG-04: a player still establishing kinesthetic control cannot allocate attention to opponent-behavior modeling — kinesthetic mastery precedes social-contingency mastery.

concepts.label: EVE Online Guiding Hand Social Club heist as betrayal exemplar
concepts.gloss: April 2005 EVE heist by mercenary corporation Guiding Hand Social Club against Ubiqua Seraph (~US$16,500 virtual assets); used to demonstrate that MMOG societies sustain consequential betrayal narratives.

concepts.label: PlayStation Home as console virtual world
concepts.gloss: Sony Home — customizable avatars, decorable apartments, trophy display, friend-invite — Calleja's example of the direction multiplayer is taking on consoles.

concepts.label: three-not-four authorial enumeration slip
concepts.gloss: Calleja writes 'four dimensions of shared involvement' but enumerates and treats only three (cohabitation, competition, cooperation). Authorial typo; no fourth dimension exists in the chapter.

positions.label: MMOGs constitute full-fledged on-line societies, not merely game systems
positions.stance: Calleja's central macro-phase claim, against framings that bracket MMOG sociality as mere game-feature.

positions.label: The magic-circle is dangerous when used to analyze or govern MMOGs
positions.stance: Critical-normative position against Salen & Zimmerman-style magic-circle conceptions when corporate platforms invoke them to cordon virtual worlds from real-world social concerns.

positions.label: MMOGs function as third places (per Steinkuehler & Williams), better at bridging than bonding
positions.stance: Endorses Steinkuehler & Williams's adaptation of Oldenburg with the bridging/bonding qualification, while flagging US-centric applicability limits.

positions.label: Player disposition is fundamentally restructured by perceived human-vs-AI status of co-agents
positions.stance: Phenomenological-empirical claim grounded in interview data and Lim & Reeves (2006) arousal/engagement findings.

positions.label: Even rudimentary AI can ground cohabitation, but persistent human-controlled agents add the reputation-and-betrayal layer
positions.stance: Two-tiered claim: media-equation (Reeves & Nass; Gerhard et al.; Calo) for minimal cohabitation; MMOG persistence for the social-bond economy.

positions.label: Spectatorship is a constitutive sub-element of cohabitation, not adjacent to it
positions.stance: Calleja treats spectator-mode trials and co-located audience effects as part of cohabitation rather than a separate axis, on grounds that they are co-presence configurations.

tensions.label: Cohabitation-as-co-presence vs shared-involvement-as-interaction
tensions.description: Calleja allows minimal-cue rudimentary-AI cohabitation (Reeves-Nass, Gerhard et al.) as shared involvement, yet also distinguishes mere co-presence from the social-bond/reputation/interdependence layer the chapter foregrounds. The boundary remains fuzzy: is ambient AI density genuinely shared involvement or only its threshold form? Calleja does not fully resolve.

tensions.label: Magic-circle critique vs designer-cultivated social ties
tensions.description: Calleja attacks Blizzard's magic-circle posture as governance-evasion (p.98) yet immediately notes the same companies 'expressly design gameplay elements to foster social ties' for retention. The critique targets the magic-circle when it cordons real-world concerns out; it does not target the deliberate design of sociality for revenue. The two coexist uneasily.

tensions.label: Three-not-four enumeration slip
tensions.description: Calleja announces 'four dimensions of shared involvement' at p.101 yet lists three (cohabitation, competition, cooperation) and delivers three subsections. Authorial typo; load-bearing for Phase 3 ontology because it reveals the dimension's internal cardinality is fixed at three, not four — spectatorship is a sub-element of cohabitation, not a separate fourth.

tensions.label: Bridging-vs-bonding qualification weakens the third-place claim
tensions.description: Steinkuehler & Williams find MMOGs better at bridging than bonding; Calleja reads this as still satisfying Oldenburg's complaint (which targets bridging deficits). Yet many of Calleja's own examples (Splate moving cross-country; Nombril's flirtation; geographic guild gatherings) describe bonding, not bridging — suggesting the bridging-only verdict undersells the chapter's evidence.

residual_phenomenology_anchor_sites.site_description: MMOGs as 'full-fledged on-line societies' with friendships, marriages, betrayals — substantive Mitsein-equivalent language (being-with-others-in-shared-persistent-world) with no Heidegger cite. Strongest Layer-A Mitsein anchor in the chapter.

Sara Andrews / Blizzard case + server-consensus self-policing — substantive das-Man-equivalent language (majority chat behavior dictating what is acceptable; conformity policing) with no Heidegger cite.

Spectatorship and performance-for-audience subsection — substantive Goffmanian dramaturgy language (performance for co-located audience, shifting from goal-directed to visually-pleasing actions; spectator-mode clan trials as institutionalized audience-screening) with no Goffman cite. This is the chapter-level Layer-A anchor site flagged by IG-03 + IG-10 propagation.
Reeves-Nass media-equation passage treating computers as social actors at minimal cues — substantive intersubjectivity-with-non-human-others language without Husserl/Schutz/Levinas cite.
Human-vs-AI agent-recognition passage — substantive intentional-stance / theory-of-other-minds language without Dennett or Husserl cite.

paradigm_worked_examples.calleja_analytic_move: Operationalizes all three sub-dimensions: cohabitation (Ironforge city avatars; Baal's 'whole living world'), cooperation (end-game guild content; PvE focus), competition (PvP servers); plus governance case (Sara Andrews) and Austin Texas geographic guild as bridging-spillover example.

Operationalizes mass-scale cooperation (Bladerunner's 'virtual armies'; Ghosts of the Revolution outfit Figure 6.3); social contingency (BunkerBoy86 human-vs-AI preference); and the cooperation-competition fusion in large-scale FPS combat.

Paradigm case of designed-interdependence cooperation: AI director, Hunter/Smoker rescue-required mechanics, see-through-walls cohesion device, single-use shared medical pack — collaboration engineered into mechanical substrate, not optional.
Co-located living-room spectatorship case: audience cheering and gasping shifts play from goal-directed to visually-pleasing — operationalizes spectatorship-as-sub-element-of-cohabitation.

Dimitri Rascalov betrayal of Nico Bellic — operationalizes media-equation cohabitation: NPC sociality processed as social-actor betrayal, not program interaction; demonstrates AI-only co-presence can still ground shared involvement.

paradigm_worked_examples.game: Counter-Strike / Call of Duty IV / Red Orchestra
paradigm_worked_examples.calleja_analytic_move: Operationalizes the casual-to-semipro arc: from random-group online play to clan-based competitive teams (Rambusch et al. 2007), institutionalizing the shift from individual to team-play identity.

paradigm_worked_examples.game: EVE Online (Guiding Hand Social Club heist)
paradigm_worked_examples.calleja_analytic_move: Operationalizes the betrayal sub-genre of macro-phase MMOG society — virtual social structure carries economic consequence sufficient to make corporate-takedown plotlines legible as social events, not technical exploits.

burke_pentad.rationale: Shared involvement is constitutively about the Agent-locus: human and AI agents in shared environments. The Agent-Scene ratio captures cohabitation; Agent-Act captures cooperation and competition; Agent-Agency captures the communication-channel infrastructure (guild chat, Ventrilo, spectator-mode).

uexkull_construct.secondary_possibility: Bedeutungsträger (meaning-carrier) as other-player — the other-player is a Bedeutungsträger whose Merktöne (perception-tones) differ qualitatively from those of an NPC Bedeutungsträger; this anchors Calleja's human-vs-AI distinction in Uexküllian terms.
uexkull_construct.rationale: Per plan §3.D.i, Shared maps to Heideggerian Mitsein, not to Umwelt/Merkwelt/Wirkwelt. A weak Uexküllian anchor remains possible via Bedeutungsträger (meaning-carrier): the other player carries differential effect-tones that distinguish them from coded NPCs, but this anchor is anticipatory only.

secondary_anchors: Heideggerian das Man (for the Sara Andrews / server-consensus governance case)
Aristotelian koinōnia / philia (for guild and friendship structures)
aristotelian_heideggerian.rationale: Shared involvement IS the chapter's strongest Mitsein bridge in the entire volume — the macro-phase 'full-fledged on-line societies' formulation and the Reeves-Nass media-equation passage both substantively describe being-with-others-in-shared-world without ever citing Heidegger. The Sara Andrews / Blizzard server-consensus passage substantively describes das-Man conformity-policing without citing Heidegger. BCAP-indexed Mitsein analysis is the natural dissertation grounding.
corpus_index_anchors: BCAP / Heidegger Sein und Zeit §§25–27 (Mitsein, Mitwelt, das Man)

Goffman is NOT cited. This is a chapter-level Layer-A residual-phenomenology anchor site per IG-03 + IG-10 propagation.
